jupyter: python3
abstract: |
    Since the release of ChatGPT, generative AI is expected to affect highly educated occupations more than earlier waves of automation. We study whether occupational exposure to generative AI is associated with the wages of tertiary-educated employees in Switzerland, and whether it improves wage prediction. We link the Swiss Household Panel (2016-2024) with the ILO (2025) exposure index through 4-digit ISCO-08 codes. Graduates work in more exposed occupations than other employees, and better-paid occupations tend to be more exposed, but only up to a point: the most exposed occupations include clerical jobs, which are only moderately paid. However, adding exposure to a wage model barely improves prediction on unseen individuals, and a placebo test and nested regressions suggest that what exposure adds mostly comes from identifying the type of occupation, even with 2-digit occupation groups. The association is weaker for young graduates, for whom it is close to zero. Following the same graduates over time, the association is smaller and less precise when each graduate is compared with themselves after a change of occupation, which suggests that part of the link across occupations reflects which workers sort into them. With only two waves after ChatGPT, these results describe associations rather than effects of AI.

# Appendices {.unnumbered}

Appendices A to E compare the relation between AI exposure and wages across subgroups of tertiary-educated employees. They use the same data and the same tools as the EDA. For each group we report the number of observations, the weighted mean exposure, the median FTE income, the Spearman correlation between exposure and log income, and the difference in median income between the most and the least exposed quintile (quintiles defined on all graduates, as in @fig-young). These are descriptive comparisons: groups also differ in age, sector and occupation. Appendix F describes the starting salaries of graduates with official data, and Appendix G gives a within-person robustness check, which compares each graduate with themselves when they change occupation.

```{python}
#| label: appendix-setup
#| output: false
def subgroup_table(groups):
    # one row per group: size, exposure, income, and the exposure-income relation
    rows = []
    for name, d in groups.items():
        rho, p = stats.spearmanr(d["exposure_mean_2025"], d["log_income"])
        med_q = d.groupby("exposure_q", observed=True)["income_fte"].median()
        rows.append({
            "Group": name,
            "Observations": len(d),
            "Persons": d["idpers"].nunique(),
            "Mean exposure (weighted)": round((d["exposure_mean_2025"] * d["wicss"]).sum() / d["wicss"].sum(), 3),
            "Median FTE income (CHF)": round(d["income_fte"].median()),
            "Spearman ρ (exposure, income)": round(rho, 3),
            "p-value": p,
            "Q5 - Q1 median income (CHF)": round(med_q["Q5 (most)"] - med_q["Q1 (least)"]),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Group")
```

## Appendix B: Age groups {#sec-app-age .unnumbered}

The EDA compares young (25-34) and older (35-65) graduates. Here we use four age groups of ten years.

```{python}

#| tbl-cap: "Exposure and wages of tertiary-educated employees, by age group"

age_names = ["25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-65"]
tert["age_group4"] = pd.cut(tert["age"], bins=age_bins, labels=age_names, right=False)
app_age = subgroup_table({name: tert[tert["age_group4"] == name] for name in age_names})
app_age
```

The median income rises with age, from CHF `{python} f"{app_age.iloc[0]['Median FTE income (CHF)']:,.0f}"` for graduates aged 25-34 to CHF `{python} f"{app_age.iloc[-1]['Median FTE income (CHF)']:,.0f}"` for those aged 55-65. The correlation between exposure and income is `{python} f"{app_age.iloc[0]['Spearman ρ (exposure, income)']:.2f}"` for the youngest group and `{python} f"{app_age.iloc[-1]['Spearman ρ (exposure, income)']:.2f}"` for the oldest (@tbl-app-age).

## Appendix C: Universities vs higher vocational education {#sec-app-tertiary .unnumbered}

Our definition of tertiary education follows the FSO and includes higher vocational education (ISCED 5B). Here we separate universities, universities of applied sciences and doctorates (ISCED 5A and 6, the stricter definition) from higher vocational education (5B).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-app-tertiary
#| tbl-cap: "Exposure and wages by type of tertiary education (ISCED 5A and 6 vs 5B)"
app_tert = subgroup_table({
    "Universities and doctorates (5A, 6)": tert[tert["isced"].isin([51, 60])],
    "Higher vocational education (5B)": tert[tert["isced"] == 52],
})
app_tert
```

The relation between exposure and income is `{python} "positive" if app_tert.iloc[0]["Spearman ρ (exposure, income)"] > 0 else "negative"` for university graduates (ρ = `{python} f"{app_tert.iloc[0]['Spearman ρ (exposure, income)']:.2f}"`) and `{python} "positive" if app_tert.iloc[1]["Spearman ρ (exposure, income)"] > 0 else "negative"` for higher vocational graduates (ρ = `{python} f"{app_tert.iloc[1]['Spearman ρ (exposure, income)']:.2f}"`) (@tbl-app-tertiary).

The FSO survey of higher education graduates (EHA) gives the standardized gross annual income (full-time equivalent) one year after graduation, for graduates working in Switzerland. It is public, aggregated data: it cannot be linked to the SHP, but it describes the starting point of the careers we study.

Starting salaries change little over time for most degrees, but not for all (@fig-app-eha-trend). The median income of university Master graduates is CHF `{python} f"{master_2024:,.0f}"` for the 2024 cohort, against CHF `{python} f"{master_2014:,.0f}"` for the 2014 cohort. In contrast, the starting salary of university Bachelor graduates falls from about CHF 80,000 (2006 cohort) to about CHF 74,000 (2024 cohort), while that of teaching diplomas rises from about CHF 86,000 (2004 cohort) to about CHF 99,000 (2024 cohort). The 2022 and 2024 cohorts, who entered the labour market after the release of ChatGPT, do not show a break in starting salaries.

Among Master graduates, Economics and business and Medicine graduates have the highest starting salaries, and Law graduates the lowest (@tbl-app-eha-field). Already one year after graduation, women earn less than men for every degree (@tbl-app-eha-sex), but the gap is small for university Master graduates compared with the gap we observe at older ages in the SHP.

As a rough consistency check, the median net FTE income of tertiary-educated employees aged 25-29 in the SHP is CHF `{python} f"{shp_young_median:,.0f}"`. This is below the EHA medians, as expected: SHP incomes are net of social contributions (roughly 12-15% of the gross wage), include higher vocational graduates, and cover several years after graduation rather than exactly one. ## Appendix G: Within-person comparison (graduates who change occupation) {#sec-app-within .unnumbered}

All the models of the main analysis compare **different** persons. If exposed occupations pay more, it may simply be because more qualified or more able persons work in them (*sorting*). The panel allows a stricter comparison: we compare **each person with themselves** in different years. Everything that does not change for a person (ability, family background, quality of the degree) then drops out, and the association is identified only by persons whose occupation, and therefore exposure, changes over time.

To do this, we subtract from each variable the mean of the person over the years (the *within* or *fixed-effects* estimator). In the model

$$
\log w_{it} = \beta \, \text{expo}_{it} + \gamma_t + \alpha_i + X_{it}'\delta + \varepsilon_{it},
$$

the person effect $\alpha_i$ is constant, so it disappears once the person mean is subtracted. The coefficient $\beta$ is then exactly the coefficient of a `LinearRegression` (course) on the demeaned data, which we compute with `groupby().transform("mean")`; we use `statsmodels` only to obtain standard errors clustered **by person**, since the observations of one person are not independent. Variables that never change for a person (sex, education level) also disappear, and linear age is dropped because, for one person, it increases exactly like the survey year.

We compare three models: (1) pooled OLS, a comparison across persons as in the main analysis; (2) person fixed effects; (3) person fixed effects plus the ISCO major group, i.e. at a constant skill level, so that promotions or moves to another type of occupation are not counted as changes in exposure. Exposure is again multiplied by 10, so the coefficient is the change in income for a 0.1 change in exposure, close to a typical change of occupation. We keep only persons observed at least two years and only exact 4-digit codes: vague codes completed with zeros (for example 2500) create artificial changes of occupation from one year to the next (@tbl-app-changers). The main sample is tertiary-educated employees; all employees are used as a robustness check.

This is a robustness check for sub-question 2; its main result is summarised in the Discussion.

### Occupation changers {.unnumbered}

Before estimating the model, we checked that enough persons change occupation, at three levels of detail: 4-digit codes (upper bound, which includes coding noise, for example the same job coded 2512 one year and 2514 the next), 2-digit groups (a different type of occupation) and major groups (a change of skill level, almost certainly real but rarer). We count these persons with all codes and with exact 4-digit codes only, because a vague code completed with zeros (for example 2000 one year, 2512 the next) creates an artificial change of occupation.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-app-changers
#| tbl-cap: "Tertiary-educated persons observed at least two years who change occupation, by level of detail of the ISCO code"
tert_panel = tert[tert.groupby("idpers")["year"].transform("nunique") >= 2].copy()
tert_panel["isco2"] = tert_panel["isco_code"].str[:2]
tert_exact = tert_panel[tert_panel["exposure_source"] == "isco4"]

changer_rows = []
for level, col in [("4 digits", "isco_code"), ("2 digits", "isco2"), ("Major group (1 digit)", "isco1")]:
    changer_rows.append({
        "Level": level,
        "All codes": int((tert_panel.groupby("idpers")[col].nunique() > 1).sum()),
        "Exact 4-digit codes only": int((tert_exact.groupby("idpers")[col].nunique() > 1).sum()),
    })
app_changers = pd.DataFrame(changer_rows).set_index("Level")
app_changers
```

Of the `{python} f"{tert_panel['idpers'].nunique():,}"` graduates observed at least two years, `{python} f"{app_changers.loc['2 digits', 'All codes']:,}"` change 2-digit group with all codes, and `{python} f"{app_changers.loc['2 digits', 'Exact 4-digit codes only']:,}"` once the vague codes are removed (@tbl-app-changers). Removing the vague codes therefore eliminates a part of the changes that only come from the coding, which is why the within-person comparison uses exact codes only.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-within-sample
#| tbl-cap: "Samples used for the within-person comparison (exact 4-digit codes, persons observed at least two years)"
within_info
```

### Results {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-within
#| tbl-cap: "Exposure and log FTE income: comparison across persons (pooled OLS) and within persons (fixed effects). Coefficient = approximate % change in income for a 0.1 increase in exposure. Standard errors clustered by person."
within_table.round(3)
```

The within-person estimates are identified by `{python} f"{n_t_changers:,}"` tertiary-educated persons (`{python} f"{n_a_changers:,}"` employees in total) whose exposure changes over the period (@tbl-within-sample); the median change is `{python} f"{within_info.loc['Tertiary-educated', 'Median size of a change in exposure']:.2f}"` on the 0-1 scale, so a change of occupation usually changes exposure by a noticeable amount.

Among graduates, an exposure 0.1 higher is associated with an income about `{python} f"{t_pooled:+.1f}"`% different when we compare different persons (model 1), and `{python} f"{t_fe:+.1f}"`% when we compare each person with themselves (model 2, p = `{python} f"{p_t_fe:.3f}"`, `{python} significance(p_t_fe)`, @tbl-within). Among all employees, the two estimates are `{python} f"{a_pooled:+.1f}"`% and `{python} f"{a_fe:+.1f}"`% (p = `{python} f"{p_a_fe:.3f}"`). When the within-person estimate is smaller than the pooled one, the difference measures the part of the link across persons that comes from **which** workers sort into exposed occupations rather than from the occupation itself. Among graduates, the within-person estimate is `{python} sorting_word` the comparison across persons. Controlling for changes in major group (model 3) gives `{python} f"{t_fe_major:+.1f}"`% for graduates (p = `{python} f"{p_t_fe_major:.3f}"`) and `{python} f"{a_fe_major:+.1f}"`% for all employees (p = `{python} f"{p_a_fe_major:.3f}"`). `{python} major_text`

These results should be read with care. Within-person estimates are imprecise, because they rely only on the persons who change occupation, and these persons are not a random subset of workers. Part of the remaining changes may still be coding noise, which pushes the estimates towards zero. Fixed effects remove what is constant for a person, but not events that happen together with the change of occupation (promotion, new employer). Finally, the ILO index is fixed in 2025: exposure changes only when the occupation changes, so these results describe wage differences between occupations, not the arrival of AI over time.

```{python}
#| label: app-within-check
#| output: false
# check: the fixed-effects coefficient is the one of a LinearRegression on the demeaned data
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

d_check = within_samples["Tertiary-educated"]
years_check = pd.get_dummies(d_check["year"], prefix="y", drop_first=True, dtype=int)
X_check = demean(pd.concat([d_check[["expo10", "age2"]], years_check], axis=1), d_check["idpers"])
y_check = demean(d_check["log_income"], d_check["idpers"])
lr_check = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(X_check, y_check)
coef_check = 100 * lr_check.coef_[0]
```

As a check of the method, a `LinearRegression` without intercept on the demeaned data gives a coefficient of `{python} f"{coef_check:+.2f}"`% for model 2, the same as `statsmodels` (`{python} f"{t_fe:+.2f}"`%, @tbl-within): `statsmodels` is used only for the clustered standard errors.
